author: Marissa Brunkhorst
title: 29 days of house-arrest for Canton reckless driving case - NewsBreak
text:
By Marissa Brunkhorst ,
6 hours ago
CANTON, S.D. (KELO) — After an Ohio man was struck and killed by a pickup while riding his motorcycle, the man who drove the truck will serve 29 days on house arrest.
Jerry Wallenstein of Canton was driving his Chevrolet Silverado traveling eastbound on U.S. Highway 18 about five miles south of Lennox. That’s when Wallenstein’s truck collided with a motorcycle while entering the left turning lane, attempting to turn north on 466th Avenue. Jerry Shafer, 60, who was on the motorcycle, died at the scene. The crash happened in July of 2024
Wallenstein admitted to reckless driving in June. In exchange, charges of vehicular homicide, DUI controlled drug and failure to yield charges were dropped.
State’s attorney Thomas Wollman said his office didn’t believe it could establish beyond a reasonable doubt that there was impairment to a degree to reach a guilty jury verdict. In turn, a plea agreement was reached with Wallenstein’s defense.
More rattlesnakes in South Dakota? On Wednesday, a judge sentenced Wallenstein to 29 days on house arrest with electronic monitoring, with one day suspended.
Two victim-impact statements were given at the sentencing hearing. The first was from Shafer’s best friend, Ken Hardesty. Shafer was traveling to Hardesty’s vacation cabin to visit him, on a cross-country road trip. Hardesty described the guilt that “hasn’t really gone away” since losing his friend and the countless memories they shared.
The second to speak was Shafer’s brother, Jeff, who called the crash a “reckless, carless act,” and asked the judge for the maximum penalty for Wallenstein.
“It’s preposterous,” he said. “The fact you can kill someone and end up with just a misdemeanor charge is ludicrous in my mind,” Jeff told KELOLAND News in June.
The maximum penalty for reckless driving in South Dakota is up to a year in jail.
“In South Dakota, we don’t have a negligent homicide law, so we’ve got this gap between reckless driving all the way up to vehicular homicide,” Wollman said.
Negligent homicide is determined when there is no premeditated intent for another person to die, but rather when someone behaves in a way that he or she should have known is risky, known as criminal negligence . Numerous states have adopted the statute.
Wollman said for crimes like reckless driving, he’s seen “a pretty broad range of sentences” that involve death in various crimes like reckless driving and vehicular manslaughter.
“We don’t have these cookie-cutter sentences for cases like this that involve death,” he said.
